newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline leads oil higher, coffee prices fall.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline leads oil higher, coffee prices fall.

text.p: Gasoline prices rose Friday as traders looked ahead to a rise in demand in the spring and summer driving season and strikes in Colombia and Venezuela helped support prices for crude oil.

Gasoline for March delivery rose 1.07 cents to 64.25 cents a gallon at the New York Mercantile Exchange. March crude oil jumped 39 cents to $22.41 a barrel and March heating oil ended 0.89 cent higher at 60.81 cents a gallon.

"We are sort of in between seasons right now and although the gasoline season has not kicked in, people are anticipating gasoline demand to rise after it has fallen so much," said John Bradberry, a dealer at Transmontaigne Products Services Inc. in Fayetteville, Arkansas.
Bradberry said gasoline demand was running near a two-year low and so traders viewed demand as having bottomed.
Also supporting prices was news Tosco Corp. prolonged a shutdown of a gasoline unit at its Martinez, California, refinery until June, two months longer than initally forecast.
The 32,000 barrel-a-day hydrocracker was shut on Jan. 21 after it exploded and burned when a hydrocarbon line ruptured.
Meanwhile, workers in Colombia including those of Ecopetrol, the state oil firm, continued their nationwide strike Friday to protest wages and privatization.
Workers for Venezuela's state oil firm PDVSA conducted an eight-hour work stoppage to protest working conditions.
There have been conflicting reports on the impact of the strikes. But private oil firms with interests in Colombia, such as British Petroleum, have said their production has been unaffected.
Elsewhere, coffee futures pulled back after rising for six straight sessions as speculators took profits ahead of the long holiday weekend.
March coffee fell 2.20 cents to 177.85 cents a pound at the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange after earlier setting a new life-of-contract high of 182.50 cents.
"It was extremely overbought going into this session," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "I think it could probably go down further next week."
Dealers said a drop was inevitable after March delivery's run-up to 21-month highs on Thursday.
Still, the March contract rose nearly 18 percent for the week and was up 70 percent for the last 2-1/2 months on worries about tight supplies and poor Latin American crops.
New York precious metals futures extended the week's recovery led by demand from professional commodity funds.
April gold rose $3.70 to $346.70 an ounce at New York's Commodity Exchange, and March silver ended up 11.0 cents at $5.252 an ounce, its highest since last September.
On Wednesday this week gold fixed at a new three-year low of $336.90 before a large-scale rally led by speculative funds led the whole precious metals complex sharply higher.

"There was heavy fund participation, some activity related to the expiry of March metals options today, and position squaring ahead of the holiday Monday," Refco New York metals analyst Tim Porter said.

March wheat added 1/2 cent to $3.59-1/2 a bushel at the Chicago Board of Trade on hopes for a large sale of U.S. wheat this weekend to Pakistan and prospects for further sales of wheat to Asian customers.
But Canadian logistical problems rattled the market.
"The Pakistan tender is supporting it but the Canadian thing isn't helping," said Ron Kucha of O'Connor and Co.
The wheat market was stirred early Friday by news Canada may seek to ship wheat through U.S. ports. Traders said that could be bearish for U.S. wheat.
Traders said it was likely Pakistan will buy 450,000 metric tons of wheat from the United States, as the Australian Wheat Board said its strong shipments may stop it from offering wheat to Pakistan.
